docs.title: qic(): methods and conformance
docs.text:
This document records how qic() computes center lines, limits and signals, which published source each choice follows, and every place it departs from that source. It is the time-series counterpart of methods.md, which covers funnels.

qic() follows R's qicharts2 [1] unless stated otherwise. tests/test_reference.py compares it with qicharts2, and with NHSRplotthedots [5] for method="nhs", on the packages' own data to 1e-6. The R output lives in fixtures/reference/ and is regenerated by scripts/make_reference_fixtures.R. Each accepted difference is listed in the test's DEPARTURES table and in §4 below.

docs.title: 1. The pipeline
docs.text:
src/qikit/spc.py runs these steps in order:

  1. Normalize. Columns or sequences become one frame. n= divides y on every chart, as in qicharts2, so an i chart of a rate is chart="i", y=events, n=cases.
  2. Aggregate. Rows that share an x become one subgroup: numerators and denominators summed, raw values combined by agg_fun=. Numeric and date x are sorted first, so runs and moving ranges follow time, not row order. Text x keeps its order. x_period= buckets dates.
  3. Baseline. freeze=k sets the limits from points 1..k. part= splits the chart into phases; part=k and freeze=k both mean "ends at point k". exclude= drops points from the limits and the rules but still draws them.
  4. Limits. core/shewhart.py, per part, from that part's baseline points.
  5. Rules. core/rules.py, per part, by method=.
  6. Table. result.data and result.summary.

docs.title: 2. Center lines and limits
docs.text:
σ̂ is estimated from the baseline points of each part.

Chart Center line σ̂ Source run median none [1] i mean screened MR̄/d₂ (MR above 3.267·MR̄ dropped, then MR̄ recomputed) [1, 2] mr MR̄ UCL = D₄·MR̄ = 3.267·MR̄, LCL = 0 [2] xbar grand mean, weighted by subgroup size Sp/c₄(d + 1), pooled over baseline subgroups [2] s c₄(nᵢ)·σ̂ as xbar [2] t i chart on y^(1/3.6), back-transformed as i [1, 3] p Σy/Σn √(p̄(1 − p̄)/nᵢ); UCL capped at 1, LCL floored at 0 [2] pp Σy/Σn Laney: σ_z·√(p̄(1 − p̄)/nᵢ) [4] c mean √c̄ [2] u Σy/Σn √(ū/nᵢ) [2] up Σy/Σn Laney: σ_z·√(ū/nᵢ) [4] g median, drawn as CL limits from the mean ḡ: ḡ ± 3√(ḡ(ḡ + 1)), LCL floored at 0 [1, 2 p. 319]

c₄ is exact, √(2/(n − 1))·Γ(n/2)/Γ((n − 1)/2), not a table. A₃, B₃ and B₄ are derived from it. The TypeScript engine computes the same function.

Laney's σ_z is the screened MR̄ of the standardized values zᵢ divided by 1.128, with no floor at 1, as in qicharts2. Under-dispersed data therefore draw limits narrower than the p or u chart. A series with every z equal has σ_z = 0 and NaN limits.

The 2σ lines (ucl_95, lcl_95) are CL ± 2σ̂ on every chart, capped like the 3σ lines. They are what the 2-of-3 rules read.

method="nhs" on an i chart uses Making Data Count's 2.66·MR̄ for the 3σ half-width, with the same screened MR̄ [5]. 3/d₂ = 2.6596, so the difference is in the fourth significant figure.

docs.title: 3. Rules (method=)
docs.text: A point beyond the 3σ limits is the chart's own test: signal = "outlier". The rules find patterns and mark the points that form them in runs_signal.

docs.title: 3.1 "anhoej" (default)
docs.text:
Anhøj and Olesen's rules [6], as qicharts2 implements them. Points on the center line are not useful and are skipped.

  • Longest run. A signal when the longest run on one side is longer than round(log₂ n) + 3, where n is the number of useful points.
  • Crossings. A signal when the number of crossings is fewer than the 5th percentile of Binomial(n − 1, ½), qbinom(0.05, n − 1, 0.5).
  • No minimum n. qicharts2 applies both rules at any n.

summary reports n_useful, longest_run, longest_run_max, n_crossings, n_crossings_min, longest_run_signal and crossings_signal. Too few crossings is a property of the whole series, so the plot can color every point (runs_highlight=).

Sensitivity. Before 1.0 qikit used floor(log₂ n) + 3 with "at least", which flags runs one or two points shorter. Simulated with the median from the same data, false signals from the run rule fall from 2–10% to 0–2% across n = 12 to 48. Power to see a 1 SD shift in the last half falls from 18% to 8% at n = 20 and from 45% to 19% at n = 48. The crossings rule still catches most sustained shifts. "nhs" or "ihi" recover the shorter run under a published rule set.

docs.title: 3.2 "nhs": Making Data Count
docs.text:
NHS England's rules for XmR charts [5, 7], as NHSRplotthedots implements them:

Rule Condition Beyond limits a point outside the 3σ limits 7-point trend 7 points in a row strictly rising or falling; a repeated value breaks it 2 of 3 near a limit 2 of 3 consecutive points beyond 2σ, all three on the same side 7 on one side 7 points in a row on one side of the mean; a point on the mean breaks it

Each point takes the first of these it belongs to, in the order of the table, as its special_cause. A point inside a trend takes the trend's direction; at the join of two trends, the one it starts.

With worse=, each point's variation is "improving", "concerning" or "common". Without it, a special cause is "neutral". summary["variation"] is the last point's, which is what the Making Data Count icon shows.

With target= and worse=, summary["assurance"] is judged at the last point's limits. It is "pass" when the target lies beyond the limit on the bad side, so the process cannot miss it by chance. It is "fail" when the target lies beyond the limit on the good side, and "variable" when it lies inside the limits.

docs.title: 3.3 "ihi": Provost and Murray
docs.text:
From The Health Care Data Guide [3]. Repeated values are passed over in a trend.

  • Run chart: a shift of 6 or more on one side of the median, and a trend of 5 or more.
  • Shewhart chart: a shift of 8, a trend of 6, 2 of 3 beyond 2σ on one side, and 15 in a row within 1σ.

The run chart's runs-count table is not implemented. Anhøj's crossings rule, the default method, answers the same question with a formula rather than a table.

docs.title: 3.4 "weco" and "nelson"
docs.text: The Western Electric zone rules [8] and Nelson's eight tests [9], less the point beyond 3σ, which is signal. Both need limits, so they do not apply to a run chart.

docs.title: 3.5 Short series: provisional and the notes
docs.text:
A chart of a few points cannot show that a process is stable, so qikit says so in words. It never changes signal, runs_signal or the limits.

Baseline points Charts What qikit does fewer than 12 all summary["provisional"] is True, a note says the series is too short to judge, and print(result) reads "No signal so far" in place of "looks stable" 12 to 19 those with control limits (not "run") a note calls the limits provisional; provisional stays False 20 or more all nothing

The count is of the points that set the current center line: the baseline points of the last part. freeze=10 therefore leaves a chart provisional however many points follow, and so does a new part (part=) that is still short.

Where the numbers come from. They are rules of thumb, set as the constants MIN_POINTS and MIN_LIMIT_POINTS in spc.py, and published guidance does not agree on one figure:

  • 20 is the usual figure for control limits from a stable baseline (Provost and Murray [3]; Montgomery [2] asks for 20 to 25 subgroups).
  • 12 is qikit's own choice. It lies between the roughly 10 points at which run-chart guidance sets a baseline median (Perla, Provost and Murray [10]) and the 15 that Making Data Count [7] asks for before drawing process limits. A team reporting under Making Data Count should read 12 to 14 points as too few for limits, which the 12-to-19 note already says.

The run rules give the practical reason for caution (§3.1): at n = 20 they have 8% power to see a 1 SD shift in the last half of the series, so no signal on a short series says little.

docs.title: 4. Departures from qicharts2
docs.text:
Each is deliberate and listed in tests/test_reference.py.

  • The MR chart's 2σ line. qikit draws MR̄(1 + 2·d₃/d₂) = 2.511·MR̄, the moving range's own 2σ. qicharts2 draws two-thirds of the UCL, 2.178·MR̄. Only ucl_95 is affected.
  • xbar with unequal subgroups. qikit uses ±3σ̂/√nᵢ with the unbiased σ̂ = Sp/c₄(d + 1), d the pooled degrees of freedom. qicharts2 uses A₃(nᵢ)·Sp, which corrects with c₄(nᵢ). The two differ by a fraction of a percent.
  • s with unequal subgroups. qikit's center line is c₄(nᵢ)·σ̂, the expected sᵢ, so it moves with nᵢ. qicharts2 draws a flat CL = Sp with B₃/B₄(nᵢ) limits. With equal subgroups the two agree.
  • A moving range across a part boundary is NaN in qikit, so one part's spread never leaks into the next. qicharts2 computes each part separately and agrees.

docs.title: 5. What changed in 1.0
docs.text:
Each change below moves results on some data. The CHANGELOG has the full list.

Change Effect on signals Run rule: round(log₂ n) + 3 with "longer than" Fewer false signals, less power (§3.1) xbar/s spread from the baseline and each part More sensitive after a real change g chart limits from the mean Limits about 10–15% wider Laney σ_z: screened, no floor Narrower limits on under-dispersed series ihi run-chart rules 6/5; zone rules on Shewhart charts More sensitive, as published n= divides y on every chart; p UCL capped at 1; MR LCL 0 None on valid data

docs.title: qikit in Snowflake
docs.text:
qikit's analysis needs only numpy and pandas, which every Snowflake Python runtime provides. import qikit does not load plotly, so a stored procedure or UDTF can compute limits without the plotting extra. Streamlit in Snowflake adds plotly for .plot().

The pattern everywhere is the same: one call, .data out.

from qikit import qic, funnel

qic(df, x="MONTH", y="NUM", n="DEN", chart="p", facets=["MEASURE", "SERVICE"]).data
funnel(df, y="OBS", n="EXP", measure="oe", unit="NPI", facets="MEASURE").data

facets= takes one column or a list. Each combination gets its own center line, limits, τ and FDR step, and the facet columns lead the output, so the result joins back to the source table on them.

docs.title: 1. Getting the package into Snowflake
docs.text:
qikit is pure Python, so either route works.

From PyPI, through the artifact repository. Where your account has Snowflake's shared PyPI repository enabled:

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE ...
  ARTIFACT_REPOSITORY = snowflake.snowpark.pypi_shared_repository
  PACKAGES = ('snowflake-snowpark-python', 'clinical-qikit')
  ...

From a stage. Build or download the wheel and upload it once:

uv build --wheel                      # dist/clinical_qikit-1.4.5-py3-none-any.whl

CREATE STAGE IF NOT EXISTS QI.PUBLIC.PY_LIBS;
PUT file://dist/clinical_qikit-1.4.5-py3-none-any.whl @QI.PUBLIC.PY_LIBS
  AUTO_COMPRESS = FALSE OVERWRITE = TRUE;

Then list it in IMPORTS and keep numpy and pandas in PACKAGES. A pure-Python wheel is a zip archive, which Python imports from directly.

docs.title: 2. Stored procedure: add limits to a metrics table
docs.text:
The simplest deployment. The procedure reads a pre-aggregated table, computes every chart in one faceted call, and writes the limits back.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE QI.PUBLIC.ADD_SPC_LIMITS(SOURCE STRING, TARGET STRING)
  RETURNS STRING
  LANGUAGE PYTHON
  RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.11'
  PACKAGES = ('snowflake-snowpark-python', 'numpy', 'pandas')
  IMPORTS = ('@QI.PUBLIC.PY_LIBS/clinical_qikit-1.4.5-py3-none-any.whl')
  HANDLER = 'run'
AS
$$
from qikit import qic

def run(session, source, target):
    df = session.table(source).to_pandas()           # MEASURE, SERVICE, MONTH, NUM, DEN
    out = qic(df, x="MONTH", y="NUM", n="DEN", chart="p",
              facets=["MEASURE", "SERVICE"]).data
    out.columns = [c.upper() for c in out.columns]
    session.write_pandas(out, target, auto_create_table=True, overwrite=True)
    return f"{len(out)} rows written to {target}"
$$;

CALL QI.PUBLIC.ADD_SPC_LIMITS('QI.METRICS.MONTHLY', 'QI.METRICS.MONTHLY_LIMITS');

The same body with funnel() writes one row per provider per measure: limits, signal, p_value, q_value, min_detectable and the shrinkage columns.

out = funnel(df, y="OBS", n="EXP", measure="oe", unit="NPI", label="PROVIDER_NAME",
             facets="MEASURE", worse="higher").data

A faceted call is the same as one call per partition: tests/test_public_api.py checks that row for row.

docs.title: 3. UDTF: limits inside a SQL pipeline
docs.text:
When the limits belong in a SQL statement rather than a separate table, a vectorized UDTF runs qic() once per partition. Each partition is one chart.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION QI.PUBLIC.QIC_P(MONTH DATE, NUM FLOAT, DEN FLOAT)
  RETURNS TABLE (MONTH DATE, Y FLOAT, CL FLOAT, UCL FLOAT, LCL FLOAT,
                 SIGNAL STRING, RUNS_SIGNAL BOOLEAN)
  LANGUAGE PYTHON
  RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.11'
  PACKAGES = ('numpy', 'pandas')
  IMPORTS = ('@QI.PUBLIC.PY_LIBS/clinical_qikit-1.4.5-py3-none-any.whl')
  HANDLER = 'QicP'
AS
$$
import pandas as pd
from _snowflake import vectorized
from qikit import qic

class QicP:
    @vectorized(input=pd.DataFrame)
    def end_partition(self, df):
        df.columns = ["MONTH", "NUM", "DEN"]
        d = qic(df, x="MONTH", y="NUM", n="DEN", chart="p").to_table()
        return d[["x", "y", "cl", "ucl", "lcl", "signal", "runs_signal"]]
$$;

SELECT m.MEASURE, m.SERVICE, l.*
FROM QI.METRICS.MONTHLY m,
     TABLE(QI.PUBLIC.QIC_P(m.MONTH, m.NUM, m.DEN)
           OVER (PARTITION BY m.MEASURE, m.SERVICE ORDER BY m.MONTH)) l;

Keep the returned columns fixed. RETURNS TABLE needs a stable schema, and some of .data's columns appear only with the option that makes them (part with part=, variation with method="nhs", target with target=). .to_table() returns every column of qikit.schema("qic") (or "funnel") on every call, in the same order and with the same types, empty where the call did not produce it: after the facets= columns and before the hover= columns. Return it whole, or select from it as above; qikit.schema() gives the names and types for the RETURNS TABLE clause. Booleans and fragility use pandas' nullable types, so an empty value is NULL.

Rows come back one per subgroup. qic() aggregates rows that share an x, so a partition with two rows for one month returns one. Aggregate in SQL first if the pipeline expects one output row per input row.

docs.title: 4. Choosing settings in a pipeline
docs.text:
• Charts by measure type. Proportions (chart="p") and O/E or rates (chart="u") need different calls. Run one call per chart type, faceted by measure.
  • Rules. method="anhoej" (the default) for run charts and general use; method="nhs" with chart="i" and worse= where boards use Making Data Count. .data then carries variation and special_cause per point, and the summary carries the assurance verdict when target= is given.
  • Baselines. A pipeline that recomputes monthly should fix the baseline with freeze=, so new points are judged against limits that do not move with them.
  • Funnels. tau_method="spiegelhalter" is the default and the right screen. funnel_sensitivity() returns one row per provider with the tier under each τ option; writing it alongside the funnel shows which flags depend on the model.

docs.title: 5. Performance
docs.text:
Case Time qic() p chart, 104 points about 1 ms 200 charts of 36 points, one faceted call about 0.15 s O/E funnel, 5,000 providers about 0.2 s Proportion funnel, 5,000 providers about 1 s O/E funnels, 200 facets of 30 providers, one faceted call about 2 s Proportion funnels, 200 facets of 30 providers, one faceted call about 3.5 s

These are laptop timings; a Snowflake warehouse is in the same range. A faceted funnel costs 10 to 20 ms per facet on top of its providers: each facet fits its own spread, contours, estimates and intervals. A faceted call runs the facets one after another, so a very large pipeline gains from the UDTF's parallel partitions.

docs.title: 6. Streamlit in Snowflake
docs.text:
Streamlit apps keep using .plot(), which returns a Plotly figure:

st.plotly_chart(qic(df, x="MONTH", y="NUM", n="DEN", chart="p").plot(title="H&P in 24 h"),
                use_container_width=True)

The app needs plotly as well as qikit. On the warehouse runtime, add plotly to the app's packages and place the qikit package folder (from the wheel or src/qikit) next to the app's main file in its stage. On the container runtime, add clinical-qikit[plot] to requirements.txt.

Upgrading an app to 1.0. Display options moved from qic() and funnel() to .plot(), and a few arguments were renamed. Every removed or renamed argument raises a TypeError that names its replacement, so running the app once lists every change to make. The CHANGELOG has the full table.

docs.title: For AI agents
docs.text:
• AGENTS.md ships inside the package. It maps each module, says which function answers which question, and lists the conventions an agent must not break. llms.txt is the same map at the repository root.
  • Docstrings are the reference. help(qikit.qic) and help(qikit.funnel) open with a decision table and document every result column.
  • Skills for Snowflake Cortex Code or any agent that loads them: skills/spc-monitoring/SKILL.md and skills/provider-funnels/SKILL.md.
  • result.brief() is what was found in about 1 KB of JSON-safe dict: the verdict or counts, the notes, and only the flagged points or providers. result.to_json() is everything; to_json(digits=4) rounds it.
  • Errors name the fix: a misspelt choice, keyword or column name suggests the closest match, choices ignore case, and removed arguments name their replacement.
  • Messy input is refused or reported, never guessed at: a missing value is not a zero, and text that is not a number is an error.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
uv sync --extra dev
uv run ruff check .
uv run mypy
uv run pytest tests/

The Python engine is authoritative. The TypeScript engine in excel-addin/packages/engine is a frozen subset, held to the same numbers by the shared JSON fixtures in fixtures/spc and fixtures/experiment. After an intentional change to math both engines have, change both and regenerate the snapshots with uv run python scripts/update_snapshots.py. fixtures/reference holds output from R's qicharts2, FunnelPlotR and NHSRplotthedots, regenerated by scripts/make_reference_fixtures.R; tests/test_reference.py checks qikit against it to 1e-6, with each accepted departure listed and explained.

To release: set __version__ in src/qikit/__init__.py, add that version's section to CHANGELOG.md, update the wheel name in docs/snowflake.md (the tests name anything left behind), regenerate the add-in's dev manifest with npm run manifest in excel-addin/ (CI fails if it is stale), merge to main, then tag the merge and push the tag.

git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "v1.4.0" && git push origin v1.4.0

release.yml runs the tests, checks the tag against __version__, publishes to PyPI by trusted publishing (no token) and opens a GitHub Release with the changelog section. The same tag publishes the Excel add-in to GitHub Pages (addin-pages.yml; see Installing QI Kit for Excel).

docs.title: Across providers: funnel()
docs.text: Each provider is plotted at its own volume, against Spiegelhalter's exact 99.8% and 95% probability contours (Statistics in Medicine 2005;24:1185-1202). Every method, reference and design choice is recorded in Methods: funnel plots and over-dispersion, including where qikit departs from the paper.

docs.title: Choosing the settings
docs.text:
You have Pass Observed events and risk-model expected events (mortality or readmission O/E) measure="oe", y=observed, n=expected Expected from an external risk model (Vizient, CMS), asking "worse than expected?" compare_to="model" (O/E against 1.0, no allowance for spread between providers) Asking "unusual among peers?" (the default question) compare_to="peers", or leave it unset Events out of cases (complication %, top-box %) measure="proportion", y=events, n=cases Events over exposure (infections per line-day) measure="rate", y=events, n=exposure A per-case amount: minutes, cost or counts per stay (EHR minutes per discharge) measure="mean", y= the amount, one row per case; or per provider y=SUM, n=COUNT(*), sum_sq=SUM(y*y) Days, or anything where one case adds many units (length of stay as O/E days) stay-level rows, one per case, and within_dispersion="estimate" The same, summed per provider in SQL so the stays never leave the warehouse one row per provider with cases= (k) and sum_sq= (SUM(POWER(obs, 2) / exp)), and within_dispersion="estimate" Stays whose variability differs by DRG or service line within_dispersion="<column>": one case-mix-weighted φᵢ per provider, from SQL Leaders will ask "is this flag one patient?" case-level rows (automatic), or max_case_y=/max_case_n= from SQL: see p_value_drop1, fragility Survey items, scored per item (HCAHPS composites) one row per survey (y = items "Always", n = items answered), measure="proportion", within_dispersion="estimate" A measure where only one direction is bad worse="higher" (mortality) or worse="lower" (top-box) Hundreds of providers, and few false alarms matter more than the drawn lines signal="fdr" Flags from the drawn lines, but the figure should show the FDR action list signal="limits" and .plot(color_by="fdr") Many very-low-volume providers diluting the FDR step fdr_min_denominator= (a volume floor for the FDR step only) To rank flagged providers for action sort by eb_excess, not raw_excess To reproduce a CQC or NHS SHMI funnel tau_method="cqc" or "shmi" Flags acted on one by one, where the stated chance-flag rate must hold tau_method="winsorized" The spread between providers known from earlier periods, or fewer than 30 providers tau=<value> (fixed in advance) "Does this flag depend on the model?" funnel_sensitivity(...) "What minimum denominator should this measure have?" r.min_denominator(reliability=0.7): the volume at which a score is reliable, and how many providers are above and below it "At what level should small providers be rolled up?" funnel_rollup(df, units=[...], ...): the same table for each level of a hierarchy "Is this provider probably worse than average?" (the CMS question) read prob_worse; signal answers "unusual among peers?" A fixed target on a proportion or rate (a 2% goal, not the peer average) center=<target> with overdispersion=False. With overdispersion=True a gap between the providers and the target widens every limit, and qikit warns A goal the best providers already reach, on a process measure (achievable benchmark of care) benchmark="abc" with worse= The same goal on an outcome (O/E mortality, LOS, readmission) benchmark="eb" with worse=

Rows that share a unit are summed, so stay-level or year-level data aggregates itself.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
r.data has one row per provider:

Column Meaning unit, label The provider and its display name y The plotted value: O/E, proportion or rate numerator, denominator The summed y= and n= (observed and expected, events and cases) cl The center line: pooled ΣO/ΣE (or Σevents/Σn) unless center= is given lower_outlier, upper_outlier The 99.8% contour at this provider's volume lower_alert, upper_alert The 95% contour p_value Exact p-value against the model the contours are drawn from; one-sided toward worse=, doubled when two-sided q_value Its Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment across the chart's providers signal "outlier", "alert" or "none". The tiers never overlap direction "higher" or "lower" than the center line min_detectable The smallest true value this provider could have flagged with 80% power ci_lower, ci_upper Exact 95% interval for the provider's own value excluded Left out with exclude= (drawn faded, not tested) raw_excess (observed − cl × denominator), signed so positive is worse: excess days or events reliability How much of the provider's difference is signal, 0–1. 0 everywhere when there is no measurable spread eb_rate, eb_excess The shrunk (empirical Bayes) value, the exact posterior mean, and its excess over the reference. Rank flagged providers on eb_excess eb_low, eb_high A 95% (interval=) interval for the provider's true value from the same posterior; NaN with no measurable spread prob_worse Posterior probability that the true value is worse than the reference (CMS-style "worse than average"); NaN with no spread estimate_flag "worse", "better" or "no different": where the interval lies against the reference ("higher"/"lower" without worse=) p_value_drop1 The p-value with the provider's single most extreme case removed (needs case rows or max_case_y=/max_case_n=); descriptive, no q-value flag_survives_drop1 For flagged providers: still flagged without that case? fragility Case rows: the fewest worst cases whose removal clears the flag (1 = one case carries it) effective_denominator Only with a within_dispersion column: n/φᵢ, the plot's x axis benchmark, meets_benchmark Only with benchmark=: the goal (same on every row of a facet), and whether this provider is at it or better benchmark_group Only with benchmark="abc": whether this provider is one of the best performers the ABC pools

r.summary holds the model and how to read the counts:

  • n_outlier, n_alert, and expected_false_flags.
  • tau: the estimated spread of true values between providers; tau_method, tau_scale, tau_source ("estimated" or "pre-specified"), tau_estimated, and tau_ci under tau_method="ml".
  • phi: the over-dispersion ratio as the chosen method defines it.
  • reference: what the estimate columns are judged against (the center line, or 1.0 under compare_to="model"), and estimate_tau, the spread of their prior.
  • count_model, limit_method, within_dispersion, dispersion_shape, underpowered, n_filtered, n_fragile.
  • With benchmark=: benchmark, a dict of method, share and value. Under "abc" it also holds:
  • providers and group_denominator: who sets it and their volumes.
  • coverage: their share of patients.
  • msd and n_below_msd: Kiefe's minimum sufficient denominator.
  • without_small: the ABC without providers below it.
  • notes: sentences ready to show a reader.

On a faceted funnel the same keys are under by_facet.

docs.title: What decides a flag
docs.text:
Each contour is the boundary of an exact test. A provider is beyond the 99.8% line exactly when its one-sided p-value is below 0.001, and beyond the 95% line exactly when it is below 0.025. For the unadjusted O/E chart that is the same as "the provider's own exact 95% interval excludes the center line". The line, the p-value, the color and the interval always agree.

signal= picks one test for both tiers:

  • "limits" (default): outlier beyond the outer contour, alert beyond the inner one. About 0.1% of average providers land beyond each 99.8% line by chance, and 2.5% beyond each 95% line. summary["expected_false_flags"] counts that for your chart. With 1,000 providers on a one-sided chart it is about 1 outlier and 24 alerts, so "35 alerts" is read against that. A point beyond the 95% line can therefore have a large q_value. For an action list use signal="fdr" or q_value; to keep signal="limits" but draw the points by their q tiers, use .plot(color_by="fdr") (below).
  • "fdr": outlier when q_value < 0.05, alert when q_value < 0.10 (fdr_levels=). At most that share of each tier is expected to be false, however many providers there are. The flags then no longer match the drawn lines, and the caption says so.

There is deliberately no "limit OR q" mode. That union only ever adds flags, so it never removes the chance alerts that make FDR worth using, and neither guarantee holds for the combined tier (methods §4.11).

limits=(0.998, 0.95) moves the contours, for example to (0.997, 0.95).

docs.title: Over-dispersion: real differences between providers
docs.text:
No risk model captures everything, so providers differ by more than chance allows. With overdispersion=True (the default) each provider is judged against that spread as well as chance, using Spiegelhalter's additive random-effects model. The smallest providers' limits barely move. The busiest level off at about the center ± z·τ instead of closing onto the line. When τ̂ is 0, which is common at physician scale, the chart is identical to overdispersion=False. That holds around the pooled center only. Around a fixed center=, τ̂ also absorbs any system-wide gap between the providers and that center, so it can be large. Every limit then widens, and qikit raises a UserWarning saying by how much (methods §4.2.1). For "worse than the risk model?" pass compare_to="model", which turns the allowance off.

How τ is estimated (tau_method=, methods §4.16):

tau_method= What it is Use when "spiegelhalter" (default) 10%-winsorized method of moments, as published Screening. The most sensitive robust option, and uncorrected like the NHS and CQC estimators "winsorized" The same with the consistency factor of his eq. 9 Flags acted on one by one, where the 0.1% and 2.5% chance rates must hold "ml" Maximum likelihood, with an interval tau_ci Data already cleaned of outliers; not robust "cqc", "shmi" CQC (√ or arcsine scale) and NHS SHMI (log scale), as FunnelPlotR computes them Reproducing those indicators (methods §4.17) tau=<value> Fixed in advance from earlier periods Fewer than 30 providers, or a stable benchmark

The published estimator understates a small real spread, so average providers flag somewhat more often than the stated rate. That is the right error for a screen whose flags are reviewed. funnel_sensitivity() runs each option and marks the providers whose tier depends on the choice:

from qikit import funnel_sensitivity

s = funnel_sensitivity(df, y="deaths", n="expected", measure="oe", unit="surgeon")
s[~s.consistent]      # flagged under one model and not another: a judgment call

Treat a non-zero τ̂ as a finding about the system: unmeasured case mix, data differences, or real variation in practice.

docs.title: Minimum denominators
docs.text:
A minimum denominator is the volume at which a provider's score is mostly signal. reliability rises with the denominator, so each reliability target has one floor, and min_denominator() returns it with its range and the providers on each side of it:

r = funnel(df, y="deaths", n="expected", measure="oe", unit="surgeon")
floors = r.min_denominator([0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
floors[["reliability", "min_denominator", "min_low", "min_high", "n_above", "n_below"]]
floors.attrs["notes"]         # cautions to show with it

The floor is in the units of n=: expected events for O/E, cases for proportions and means, exposure for rates. 0.7 is the usual target for high-stakes use; the target is a decision about the use, not a statistical result. When the data show no spread between providers there is no floor, and the result says so instead of inventing one.

To decide where to roll small providers up to, compare the levels of the hierarchy. Each level is fitted separately, because the spread between groups is not the spread between physicians:

from qikit import funnel_rollup

funnel_rollup(df, units=["surgeon", "practice", "hospital"], reliability=0.7,
              y="deaths", n="expected", measure="oe")

Methods §4.14 has the formula.

docs.title: Length of stay and other clustered counts
docs.text:
A funnel of observed/expected patient-days treats every day as an independent event. Days come in stays, so a provider's day total varies 5–10 times more than that assumption allows. Every small provider's limits come out far too narrow, and every p-value and q-value too small. τ cannot absorb this, because the missing variance shrinks with volume while τ does not.

Pass stay-level rows and let qikit measure it:

stays = session.sql("""
    SELECT provider_id, provider_name, los_days, expected_los_days
    FROM inpatient_stays WHERE discharge_date >= '2026-01-01'
""").to_pandas()

r = funnel(stays, y="LOS_DAYS", n="EXPECTED_LOS_DAYS", measure="oe",
           unit="PROVIDER_ID", label="PROVIDER_NAME",
           within_dispersion="estimate", worse="higher")
r.summary["within_dispersion"]     # φ̂: how much more variable each count is than Poisson

Decide which question the chart answers before looking, and say it in the call:

args = dict(y="LOS_DAYS", n="EXPECTED_LOS_DAYS", measure="oe", unit="PROVIDER_ID",
            within_dispersion="estimate", worse="higher")

# Is this provider unusual among its peers? Pooled ΣO/ΣE center, spread allowed.
peers = funnel(stays, **args, compare_to="peers")

# Do this provider's stays run longer than the risk model (Vizient, CMS) expects?
model = funnel(stays, **args, compare_to="model")

If the whole system runs long against the model, model flags many providers and peers few: that gap is a finding about the system, not about one provider. Passing center=1.0 alone answers neither question (see the over-dispersion section above).

  • The estimate: φ̂ comes from each stay's residual around its own provider's rate, so real differences between providers stay with τ.
  • Already-aggregated data: pass a number, computed once in SQL: SUM(POWER(los - exp_los, 2) / exp_los) / (COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT provider)).
  • Event counts (deaths, readmissions) need nothing; leave the default of 1.
  • The guard: if the spread looks clustered and within_dispersion was left at 1, qikit raises a UserWarning and says so in summary["notes"] and on the figure.
  • Upstream choices: cap extreme stays at a stated percentile before aggregating. If φ̂ differs a lot between service lines, facet by service line; "estimate" is then taken per facet.
  • Multi-item surveys are the same problem on a proportion: one patient answers the three doctor questions alike, so item counts look like more data than they are. Pass one row per survey with within_dispersion="estimate"; the model then sees y/φ̂ out of n/φ̂ (Rao–Scott effective counts), interpolated rather than rounded (methods §4.13).

In one simulated length-of-stay cohort of 1,000 providers with no real differences between them, the chart flags 24 outliers and 65 alerts without the fix. With within_dispersion="estimate" it flags 3 and 20, against 1 and 24 expected by chance (methods §5 has the full simulation).

docs.title: Physician-level comparison: what the chart could not find
docs.text:
At individual-physician volumes a funnel is mostly a test with no power. The chance of flagging a physician whose true O/E is 2.0 at the 99.8% limit:

Expected deaths 2 5 10 20 50 Chance of flagging a true O/E of 2.0 5% 21% 44% 81% 99.8%

Most physicians sit at 5–20 expected events, so absence of a signal is not evidence of acceptable performance. That is exactly how a blank funnel tends to get read. So every provider carries min_detectable and an exact interval. summary["underpowered"] says whether the typical provider could detect even a doubling, and an underpowered figure captions itself so the caveat survives a slide deck. A physician at O/E 2.5 whose min_detectable is 4.6 has not been cleared; the chart cannot see that far at their volume.

The workflow that works is to aggregate until the chart has power. With the bundled example (24 surgeons, 3 years):

import pandas as pd
from qikit import funnel

df = pd.read_csv("data/examples/physician_mortality_oe.csv")

# Any single year: no outlier, and underpowered is True.
funnel(df[df.year == 2025], y="observed_deaths", n="expected_deaths",
       measure="oe", unit="physician").summary["underpowered"]       # True

# All three years (rows per physician are summed): three real signals, SURG-07 and
# SURG-15 above, and a high performer, SURG-21, below the lower limit.
r = funnel(df, y="observed_deaths", n="expected_deaths", measure="oe", unit="physician")
r.data[r.data.signal != "none"]

Physician scores are less reliable than they look. Hofer et al. found that physicians accounted for a small share of the variation in diabetes care, that reliability at typical panel sizes was low, and that a physician could improve a report card by dropping a few of their sickest patients (JAMA 1999). The fragility and p_value_drop1 columns exist for that last point. For hospitalists, Goodwin et al. found meaningful variation in length of stay and discharge destination but very little in 30-day readmission or mortality, and much of the hospitalist variation was explained by the hospital (J Gen Intern Med 2013). Expect low reliability for physician readmissions, and facet by hospital or campus (facets=) before comparing physicians.

docs.title: Estimates with a range
docs.text:
Every funnel also gives each provider a shrunk estimate with an interval, the output a CMS-style hierarchical model reports (Keenan et al., Circ Cardiovasc Qual Outcomes 2008), without writing one. A provider's true value has an exact posterior under the funnel's own model, and the interval is from that posterior:

from qikit import funnel

r = funnel(stays, y="READMIT", n="VIZIENT_EXPECTED", measure="oe",
           unit="ATTENDING_NPI", label="ATTENDING_NAME",
           compare_to="model", worse="higher")
r.data[["label", "y", "eb_rate", "eb_low", "eb_high", "prob_worse", "estimate_flag"]]
r.plot(kind="caterpillar")
  • What the interval means. eb_low–eb_high is a 95% (interval=) range for the provider's true value. Low-volume providers are pulled most toward the center line (under compare_to="model", toward the system's pooled value). Shrunk estimates are steadier and forecast next year's performance better than raw ones, especially at low volume (Dimick et al., Health Serv Res 2010). The pull also means a small provider's interval usually crosses the reference. That is "not enough data", not "fine".
  • estimate_flag and signal answer different questions. signal asks whether a provider is unusual given chance and the spread between providers. estimate_flag asks whether its true value is clearly above or below the reference (1.0 against the risk model, else the center line). Neither replaces the other, and estimate_flag has no multiplicity control: across many average providers about 5% of intervals miss.
  • Against the risk model, the limits and signal stay exactly those of compare_to="model" (1.0, no spread). The estimates shrink toward the pooled value, so a whole system running long shows every provider above 1.0, with the worst leading.
  • No measurable spread, and the interval columns are empty with a note. Pass tau= from earlier periods, or compare within a larger peer group.
  • The caterpillar plot sorts providers by eb_rate, draws each interval as a bar colored by estimate_flag, the raw value as a faint circle, and the reference as a dotted line. Ranks are very uncertain even when real differences exist (Marshall and Spiegelhalter, BMJ 1998), so read the intervals, not the order. With hundreds of providers, top= and bottom= keep the ends, and only flagged providers are named.

The spread of the prior is estimated by maximum likelihood whatever tau_method the limits use: the published estimator understates it and would leave 95% intervals covering as few as half of true values (methods §4.14, §5).

For your own risk model or covariates, the notebook docs/examples/hierarchical_readmissions.ipynb fits the full patient-level hierarchical model in PyMC (installed separately), with an optional hospital level, next to the funnel() equivalent, and compares the two.

docs.title: An achievable goal: benchmark=
docs.text:
The center line is the average, and the average is not a goal. benchmark= adds one the best providers in the same data already reach:

  • "abc", the achievable benchmark of care (Kiefe et al. 1998), for process measures. It is the pooled rate of the best providers who together hold at least 10% of patients. Providers are ranked by (x + 1)/(n + 2) so that 3 of 3 cannot top the list on luck.
  • "eb", for outcomes. It is the 90th percentile, toward better, of the shrunk estimates eb_rate (O'Brien et al. 2008).
r = funnel(df, y="hp_within_24h", n="admissions", measure="proportion", unit="physician",
           worse="lower", benchmark="abc", multiply=100)
b = r.summary["benchmark"]
b["value"]                           # e.g. 97.0: the % the best physicians achieve
r.data[r.data.benchmark_group]       # who set it
b["without_small"]                   # does it lean on low-volume physicians?
r.plot()                             # the benchmark as a dashed line

funnel(df, y="deaths", n="expected", measure="oe", unit="surgeon", worse="higher",
       benchmark="eb").summary["benchmark"]["value"]   # an achievable O/E

The ABC's authors designed it for process measures. They urge extreme caution with outcomes, and discourage its use for pay, credentialing or public report cards (methods §4.18). Both are goals for confidential feedback, not tests, so signal is unchanged.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
HOUSE = {"font": {"family": "Segoe UI", "size": 13}, "limits": {"color": "#555"}}

r.plot(
    styles=[HOUSE, {"lcl": {"visible": False}, "lcl_95": {"visible": False}}],
    x_range=(2, None),          # start at 2 expected deaths; the y axis refits
    label_signals="outlier",
    width=1000, height=560,
)

r.plot(color_by="fdr", fdr_watch=0.20)   # points by q tier; the lines stay the 95%/99.8% limits
  • Defaults for a projector: contours at 3.5:1 contrast, the 95% line dashed, points at 0.85 opacity, and the legend on. Outliers are red circles and alerts amber diamonds, so the tier never depends on color alone.
  • Axes and caption: the y axis is fitted to the providers and the narrow end of the funnel, not its low-volume flare. An unset caption states the flag rule.
  • Color by q: r.plot(color_by="fdr") colors points by their q tiers (fdr_levels) on a signal="limits" result, so the figure matches a q_value action list while r.data["signal"] and the drawn lines stay as they are. fdr_watch=0.20 adds a pale open-diamond watch tier for q < 0.20, on the figure only.
  • styles= restyles by role: data, outlier, alert, watch, runs, improving, concerning, neutral, cl, ucl, lcl, ucl_95, lcl_95, target, the groups limits and limits_95, end_labels and font. A list of dicts is merged in order, so a house style is one constant.
  • r.limits(n=None) returns the contours at any denominators, for drawing elsewhere.
  • r.min_denominator(reliability=0.7) returns the minimum denominator for one or more reliability targets, with the count of providers above and below it.
  • Unknown names raise. An unknown .plot() option raises TypeError.

docs.title: In Snowflake
docs.text: qic(...).to_table() and funnel(...).to_table() are the tables a pipeline writes back: every column of qikit.schema("qic") or qikit.schema("funnel"), in the same order and with the same types on every call (.data holds only the columns that call produced). With facets= a list of columns, one call covers every measure and service line, and the facet columns stay in the output, so the result joins back to the source table. .facet_summary() is one summary row per facet. qikit in Snowflake has a stored procedure and a UDTF that add limits to a pre-aggregated metrics table, packaging steps, and Streamlit in Snowflake notes.

docs.title: Over time: qic()
docs.text:
You have, per period chart= y=, n= Any measure, few assumptions (start here) "run" y One continuous value (LOS, wait time, O/E) "i" y Events out of cases (H&P in 24 h, mortality) "p" events, cases The same, n in the thousands (over-dispersed) "pp" events, cases (Laney) Events over exposure (infections per line-day) "u" events, exposure The same, exposure in the thousands "up" events, exposure (Laney) An O/E ratio over time "u" observed, expected Counts with constant opportunity "c" count Several raw values per period "xbar", "s" raw values, x = period Cases or days between rare events "g", "t" cases or days between The moving range of an i chart "mr" y

Rows that share an x are aggregated into one subgroup. Numeric and date x are sorted. x_period="month" buckets dates.

Rules (method=):

  • "anhoej" (default): qicharts2's run rules. A run on one side of the center line longer than round(log₂ n) + 3, or fewer crossings than the 5th percentile of Binomial(n − 1, ½).
  • "nhs": NHS England's Making Data Count, for XmR boards. A point beyond the limits, 7 on one side, 7 rising or falling, or 2 of 3 near a limit. With worse=, each point is classed improving, concerning or common cause; with target=, the summary gives the assurance verdict (pass, fail or variable).
  • "ihi": Provost and Murray. "weco", "nelson": the classic zone rules.

Baseline and phases. freeze=k sets the limits from points 1..k and judges later points against them. part= splits the chart into phases, each with its own center line, limits and rules. exclude= drops points from the limits and the rules.

qic() reproduces qicharts2 to 1e-6 on its own data. Where it departs, and why, is in qic(): methods and conformance.
